findings.title: Local cache is populated before DB write, letting limit-blocked devices bypass limit
findings.body: tagDeviceUI() checks localCache, then calls localCache.SetDefault(key) before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(). If CreateOrUpdateDevice fails with ErrDeviceLimitReached, the cache entry remains. The next request for the same new deviceID will hit the cache and return nil without touching the DB, so Authenticate will succeed. A rejected device is therefore only rejected once per ~29m cache TTL and then allowed, defeating the device limit.

findings.title: Expired devices can never re-register once limit is reached
findings.body: When count >= deviceLimit, CreateOrUpdateDevice delegates to updateDevice which does UPDATE ... WHERE device_id=? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?. A device that exists but whose updated_at is older than anonymousDeviceExpiration (30d) matches 0 rows, so updateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. The count query only counts active devices in the last 30d, so this stale device is not counted but is still rejected and can never be re-inserted/updated. Returning devices after expiry are permanently locked out while the limit is saturated.

findings.title: Count-then-write limit check is racy and unenforceable under concurrency
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice does CountDevices() then, in a separate session/statement, either updateDevice or INSERT. There is no transaction, row lock, or unique-count constraint. Concurrent anonymous logins can both observe count < limit and both INSERT, overshooting the limit. Conversely two concurrent inserts for the same new device can race. The limit cannot be reliably enforced with this check-then-act pattern.

findings.title: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService signature breaks DI/wire contract
findings.body: ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its third parameter from anonStore anonstore.AnonStore (interface) to sqlStore db.DB and now constructs the store internally with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit. Any wire provider, test, or downstream (e.g. enterprise) constructing the service by injecting a mocked AnonStore will fail to build. It also removes the ability to decorate/mock the store and couples the service to a concrete DB, an unnecessary breaking API change; the limit could be passed as a separate param while keeping the store injectable.
